faqs.a: ULID stands for Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier. It is a 26-character ID made of a 48-bit millisecond timestamp plus 80 bits of random data, encoded in Crockford Base32. Because the timestamp comes first, ULIDs sort in the order they were created.

Use ULID when you want IDs that sort by creation time, are shorter (26 vs 36 characters) and are URL-safe. Use UUID when you want the widest library support or must not expose creation time. Both are effectively collision-free.
faqs.q: ULID vs UUID: which should I use?

faqs.a: The random 16 characters are drawn from crypto.getRandomValues(), which is a cryptographically secure random source in every modern browser. They are suitable for IDs; they are not passwords or secret tokens, so treat them as public identifiers.
Only if both the millisecond timestamp and all 80 random bits match, which has a probability of about 1 in 1.2 million billion billion for the same millisecond. In practice, collisions do not happen.
ULIDs use Crockford Base32, which deliberately drops I, L, O and U because they are easy to confuse with 1, 1, 0 and V. This makes ULIDs safer to read aloud or copy by hand.
faqs.q: Why are the letters I, L, O and U missing?

faqs.a: Decode the first 10 characters as a Base32 number using the Crockford alphabet. The result is the Unix timestamp in milliseconds. This tool shows the decoded creation time next to every generated ULID.

keyFacts: A ULID is exactly 26 characters long, using the Crockford Base32 alphabet (digits plus letters, excluding I, L, O and U to avoid confusion).
The first 10 characters encode a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, so ULIDs generated later always sort after earlier ones.
The last 16 characters hold 80 bits of cryptographically secure random data, making collisions practically impossible.
ULIDs are URL-safe and case-insensitive: they need no special encoding in links, file names or query strings.
Unlike UUIDs, ULIDs reveal their creation time and sort naturally, which makes database indexing and log reading simpler.
The randomness in this tool comes from the browser's crypto.getRandomValues(), the same secure source used by password managers.

ulid-generator.workedExample:
The first 10 characters of a ULID encode the timestamp. Take "01ARZ3NDEK": in Crockford Base32, 0=0, 1=1, A=10, R=24, Z=31, 3=3, N=21, D=13, E=14, K=19. Multiply each value by the matching power of 32 and add them:
1 x 32^8 + 10 x 32^7 + 24 x 32^6 + 31 x 32^5 + 3 x 32^4 + 21 x 32^3 + 13 x 32^2 + 14 x 32 + 19 = 1469922850259
That is 1,469,922,850,259 milliseconds since the Unix epoch (30 July 2016). The remaining 16 characters carry the 80 bits of random data.
